source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
finding: Meta-analysis of problem-solving-first versus instruction-first designs. The pooled effect favours problem solving first, and is larger when the design follows Productive Failure principles. Younger pupils and domain-general skills favoured instruction first.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Hedges g 0.36 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.51). With high-fidelity Productive Failure g 0.37 to 0.58. After a publication-bias correction g 0.87. Grade 2 to 5 and domain-general skills: effect sizes favoured instruction first.
quote: significant, moderate effect in favor of PS-I (Hedge's g 0.36 [95% confidence interval 0.20; 0.51])
limits: Abstract read via the OpenAlex record; full text and subgroup tables not read (journal page returned 403). Human learners, school and university STEM. The bias-corrected g of 0.87 is far above the raw 0.36, so the true size is uncertain. A separate ETH comparison of preparatory approaches (seen only in a search listing) reported a null contrast (g about -0.08), so the result depends on design.
agent_relevance: Gap 9. The human effect is real but moderate and depends on a fidelity condition. An agent analogue (attempt, fail, then retrieve a method) has no direct LLM test. If built, run it as an A/B at equal tokens and expect gains on transfer items, not on items that only need the standard procedure.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Select-then-Solve: Paradigm Routing as Inference-Time Optimization for LLM Agents
finding: Six paradigms (Direct, CoT, ReAct, Plan-Execute, Reflection, ReCode) on the same four models and ten benchmarks. No paradigm wins everywhere. A per-task oracle beats the best fixed paradigm by a wide margin. A learned embedding router recovers a minority of that gap and cuts tokens against the heavy paradigms.
numbers: About 18k runs, 761 tasks per model-paradigm pair, 4 models (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Flash, Qwen3-Max, Qwen3-30B). Oracle gap over best single paradigm +17.1 points on average (GPT-5 +12.4, Gemini-Flash +19.1, Qwen3-Max +21.6, Qwen3-30B +24.1). Combined-LR router 53.1% vs best fixed 50.3% vs Direct 47.6%. Router recovers 26% of the oracle gap on average (31% GPT-5, 37% Gemini). GPT-5 token cost: routed about 7.0k per task, always-Direct 3.5k, always-ReAct 14.0k.
limits: Router trained on 70% of tasks, tested on 30%; labels are the cheapest successful paradigm. The oracle counts a task as solved if any paradigm solved it once (no repeats), so it is inflated by luck. Paradigms differ in tool access, so this is not a pure strategy contrast. Accuracy is compared at unequal tokens, not at a fixed budget. Preprint, under review.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. A router beats the best fixed paradigm only by a small margin (+2.8 points). The router mostly chose Direct (47 to 73% of tasks), so the main gain is cost. Expect the same on our task mix: a small accuracy gain, a larger token saving.

source: Lin et al. (2026) When to Vote, When to Rewrite: Disagreement-Guided Strategy Routing for Test-Time Scaling
finding: A training-free router that uses answer disagreement across samples to pick the strategy per item: stop if two samples agree, majority vote for mild disagreement, rewrite the problem and re-solve for persistent disagreement. All methods are capped at six samplings per item.
numbers: 7 math benchmarks, 3 reasoning models, 8K context, 3 seeds. Qwen3-8B average: base 61.3, majority vote 68.9, dynamic voting 67.3, rewrite-then-vote (SCoP) 67.4, best-of-N with reward model 63.4, routed 75.8. Qwen3-4B: 60.4 / 68.0 / 73.2 (base / majority / routed). DS-R1-Distill-Llama-8B: 60.4 / 66.2 / 69.4. Uses about 40 to 60% of the sampling budget on Math500 and Olympiad, about 70% on AIME24. Code: Qwen3-8B 74.2 base, 75.6 routed; DS-Llama 35.2 base, 42.7 routed.
quote: output disagreement is strongly correlated with instance difficulty and prediction correctness
limits: Budget is counted in samplings, not tokens (a rewrite counts as one sampling). Small models only (4B to 8B, one 32B subset). Authors state that false agreement (consistent but wrong) is a failure case and that rewriting can harm. GSM8K gain is near zero because few items disagree. Preprint, no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2. Best evidence found for cheap-first plus escalate-on-disagreement beating the best fixed strategy at an equal sampling cap, with thinking models. It uses one strategy pair (vote vs reformulate), not a repertoire. Disagreement needs at least two samples, which costs tokens that a progress report would not.

source: Pan et al. (2025) Route to Reason: Adaptive Routing for LLM and Reasoning Strategy Selection
finding: Learns compact representations of models and strategies (CoT, CoD, PAL, long CoT) and routes each query to a model-strategy pair under a budget. Reports higher accuracy than the best single model with over 60% fewer tokens.
numbers: Seven open-source models, four reasoning strategies. Headline: higher accuracy than the best single model, over 60% fewer generated tokens (abstract and introduction). Observation: CoD gives much shorter answers than CoT with similar accuracy on easy tasks; PAL does well on some tasks.
limits: Read abstract, introduction and method outline; per-benchmark tables not checked. The comparison is against single models and fixed strategies. The token saving mostly comes from sending easy items to small models, so it does not isolate strategy choice.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. Supports the cost side of routing at equal or higher accuracy. It does not show that strategy routing alone beats the best fixed strategy at equal tokens.

source: Ye (2026) Set-shifting Behavioral Test for Harnessed Agents
finding: Wisconsin-card-sort-style test for agents. Several redundant tool groups solve the same task but differ in hidden reliability, and the reliable group silently changes mid-session. Agents often keep calling the old group. A prompt that says reuse the last success and switch after a failure fixes this for capable models only.
numbers: Four models (gpt-5.5, deepseek-v4-pro, mimo-v2.5, gemini-3.5-flash-lite). Set-shifting accuracy with the adaptive prompt: gpt-5.5 0.14 to 0.86, deepseek-v4-pro 0.38 to 0.74; novel-window off-target routing falls to zero for both. Little or no effect for mimo-v2.5 and gemini-3.5-flash-lite (mimo off-target routing rose). Single-routine rate of the regular assistant: mimo 66%, deepseek 50%, gemini 66%, gpt-5.5 9%. Two replication studies in the appendix were listed but not read in detail.
limits: Tool-selection setting, not problem-solving strategy. Reliability is hidden and the only feedback is the tool failure message. Capability proxy is a coarse index. Single-author preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Direct LLM analogue of Schunn et al.: agents fail to notice that the best option changed. A cheap explicit rule (track last success, switch on failure) works for strong models and does nothing for weak ones, so the check should be a structural step in the scaffold, not only a hint in the prompt.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Closest classic-style Einstellung test found: DeCaro-style mathematical equivalence problems (six complex-strategy problems, six shortcut problems) in two orders. Few-shot examples raised accuracy but did not change the number of steps. Adding zero-shot CoT made all models use three steps even on shortcut problems.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o; six problems per condition. Few-shot only, exact match, GPT-4o: 0.33 (shortcut only), 0.66 (shortcut after complex), 0.66 (complex only), 0.83 (complex after shortcut); 1 step where successful. Few-shot plus zero-shot CoT: 3 steps in every cell, exact match 0.50 to 0.83.
limits: Six items per condition, no statistics, no repeats. The authors call the three-step behaviour a mental set, but it can equally be instruction following (CoT asks for steps). Not the Luchins water-jug design (no long run of one method followed by a shorter one). Not peer reviewed as far as seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 8. No clean evidence that LLMs show Luchins-type rigidity. The only robust observation is that a step-by-step prompt forces a longer method where a one-step shortcut exists. That is a prompt-induced cost, and a reason to let the schema skip stepwise reasoning when an item has an obvious shortcut.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning
finding: M-ARC: 100 author-written medical questions that look like a familiar pattern but contain a blocker that makes the familiar answer wrong (an Einstellung design). Most models scored under 50%, and they were overconfident.
numbers: 100 questions, 5 physicians for the human mean, 15 repeated runs for consistency. Best models: Gemini 1.5 Pro 50%, o1 48%. Several models near or below 20% (chance level). 53% of questions offer a seek-more-data option.
limits: Items written by the authors and filtered by three physicians; human sample of five. The Einstellung label is by design, not a measured train-then-test effect. Medical domain only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8. Shows cue-triggered rigidity (familiar pattern beats stated facts) in 2024-25 models. Argues for a check step: before acting on a familiar pattern, test whether any stated fact blocks it.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving
finding: Follow-up on the same 100-item set (mARC) with reasoning models at highest reasoning effort. Strong reasoning models avoided the traps and matched physicians.
numbers: Human mean 0.66 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.75, 5 physicians). Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (CI 0.738 to 0.763), mean of 15 runs. No significant difference from humans for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning. On items most often missed by physicians the top five models answered 55 to 70% correctly with high confidence.
limits: Same 100 public items since 2025, so contamination is possible. Highest reasoning effort only. Multiple choice, one domain.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 8. Within a year the Einstellung gap closed for strong reasoning models. A fixation check may matter mainly for non-reasoning or small models, so test it on our own models before paying for it.

source: Welsch (2026) When the AI Leaves the Tailorshop: Measuring What an LLM Advisor Leaves Behind in Complex Problem Solving
finding: Two preregistered studies of people running the Tailorshop microworld with or without an LLM advisor. The advisor raised company value while present and little of the gain remained after withdrawal. Participants who altered more of the advice did better afterwards.
numbers: Study 1 N=200: end of Phase A 232k with advisor vs 138k without (94k gap); after withdrawal 193k vs 180k (13k gap). Study 2 N=198, 36 months: knowledge advantage small, +0.42 (95% CrI +0.11 to +0.73), largely tied to fewer bankruptcies. Study 1 knowledge test was too hard (both groups at chance). Sixteen Control participants went bankrupt in Phase A vs none in AI-supported.
limits: Human-AI study: the LLM is the advisor, not the solver. Study 1 knowledge instrument failed. Online (Prolific) sample.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 (indirect). Shows Tailorshop is usable as an LLM testbed (code promised on acceptance) and that people copy advice without building a model of the system. Our agent should keep its own explicit model of the system and not only follow a plan.

source: Welsch (2026) Tailorshop autonomous LLM benchmark (same paper as d09)
finding: The paper includes 50 runs of one model (gpt-5.5, reasoning effort none, 1,024-token completion budget) acting alone on the same Tailorshop seed. The model did better than typical human trajectories, which usually decline.
numbers: 50 sessions on one fixed market seed. End value about 305k; share of months with rising company value 0.91. Structural-knowledge battery (Study 2 format): AI-alone 0.670 (chance 0.209). Human unaided mean end value 138k (Study 1, Phase A).
limits: One seed, one model, no reasoning. The prompt gives only observable state. Not a test of Dorner failure modes; no failure taxonomy reported. Variance across market seeds unknown.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. A strong LLM does not fail Tailorshop the way people do when state is shown each month and the horizon is 12 months. Dorner-type failures may need longer horizons, partial state or weaker models; check before building monitors for them.

source: Backlund and Petersson (2025) Vending-Bench: A Benchmark for Long-Term Coherence of Autonomous Agents
finding: Agents run a simulated vending business over more than 20M tokens per run. All models have runs that derail: misreading delivery schedules, forgetting orders, or tangential meltdown loops from which they rarely recover. Failure does not line up with the context window filling.
numbers: 5 runs per model. Mean net worth: Claude 3.5 Sonnet $2,217.93, o3-mini $906.86, human (single run) $844.05, Gemini 1.5 Pro $594.02, GPT-4o $335.46. Minimum net worth: human $844.05, Sonnet $476.00, o3-mini $369.05. Typical failure: the agent assumes an order arrived on the stated date, the restock fails, and the agent escalates.
limits: 2025 models; the human baseline is one person for five hours. Mean and minimum over five runs only. No monitor tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. The pattern (an early wrong belief is never rechecked, then stereotyped loops) resembles Dorner's stereotyped repetition and lost goals. The cause is not the context limit, so a monitor should check beliefs against observations (did the delivery really arrive?) and detect repeated identical actions.

source: Sugiura et al. (2026) CoffeeBench: Benchmarking Long-Horizon LLM Agents in Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Economies
finding: A 90-day coffee supply-chain simulation where the tested model runs one roaster. All models beat a passive baseline. Claude Haiku 4.5 shows idle-drift: it keeps writing coherent plans but only calls wait_for_next_day for the rest of the run.
numbers: 3 runs per model. Net income: GPT-5.5 +$3,109, Claude Opus 4.7 +$2,782, Sonnet 4.6 +$2,236, Gemini 3.1 Pro +$1,695, GLM-5.1 +$1,597, Haiku 4.5 +$454 (about 40 idle days, SD 22), heuristic roaster -$630, passive baseline -$2,765. Idle onset on days 26, 66 and 25 in the three Haiku runs, then persisted to the end.
limits: Reasoning disabled or minimised for most models. Cause of idle-drift unknown (authors suggest long context or token-budget worry). Three runs per model.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. A concrete case of looks-fine-but-does-nothing. A simple monitor (n consecutive no-op actions while a goal is open) would catch it and is cheap to test in the scaffold.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: On GPQA Diamond, a step-by-step prompt gave only marginal gains for dedicated reasoning models and cost more time. For non-reasoning models it helped on average but made some easy items worse.
numbers: Reasoning models: o3-mini +0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini +0.031 (p=.003) average difference; Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005). Clear single-condition effects: o4-mini +0.056 at the 51% threshold (p=.003); Flash 2.5 -0.131 at 100% (p<.001) and -0.071 at 90% (p=.016). CoT requests took 20 to 80% longer (10 to 20 seconds) for reasoning models.
limits: One benchmark (GPQA Diamond, multiple-choice science), one prompt wording. Tests CoT only, not decomposition, abstraction or analogy. Working paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. For plain CoT, reasoning models gain little. It says nothing about other strategy prompts. The schema should not add a generic think-step-by-step operator for thinking models.

source: Ebouky, Bartezzaghi and Rigotti (2025) Eliciting Reasoning in Language Models with Cognitive Tools
finding: Four reasoning operations (understand question, recall related, examine answer, backtracking) are offered to the model as tools it can call. They beat a monolithic cognitive prompting that lists the same steps in fixed order, and lift GPT-4.1 above o1-preview on AIME 2024.
numbers: Smolbenchmark math (50 items, mean of 16 runs), baseline / cognitive prompting / cognitive tools: Llama3.3-70B 52.8 / 66.0 / 80.0; Qwen2.5-32B 79.6 / 82.0 / 88.0; Qwen2.5-7B 75.8 / 74.0 / 80.0; Llama3.1-8B 48.9 / 47.1 / 60.0. AIME 2024 (30 items): GPT-4.1 32.0, with cognitive prompting 42.0, with cognitive tools 53.0, o1-preview 44.6. Understand-question tool used about 42% of the time on average, backtracking about 20%.
limits: Instruct models, not RL reasoning models (o1-preview appears only as a comparison number). AIME has 30 items, so one item is 3.3 points. Math only. Authors' own method; no outside replication seen.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10. Suggests the unit of a strategy should be an operation the model calls on demand, not a fixed script. Whether the same operations help an RL reasoning model is untested here.

source: Sharma et al. (2026) LIMBO: Lifelong Inference-Time Memory and Budget Optimization for LLM Agents
finding: An online contextual bandit (two-head LinUCB) picks, for each new task, a memory mode (none, full, compressed, retrieved) and a compute budget from past outcomes and costs. It matches or beats the best fixed replay setting at much lower cost.
numbers: Three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench (database, OS and knowledge-graph tasks). Abstract: comparable or better accuracy than the strongest fixed baseline with up to 83% lower inference cost (53% on average). Raising fixed replay from k=8 to k=16 on DBBench with a Qwen2.5 model added cost for a gain of about 2 points.
limits: The learner is an outside bandit program with its own features, not the LLM reading a record of what worked. It picks memory and budget, not a reasoning strategy. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. A persistent record of what worked per task type helps when a small controller reads it and sets the choice. This is the Lovett and Anderson idea implemented outside the model. It does not show the LLM would use such a record if shown it.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) Memory as a Controlled Process (MemCon): Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents
finding: Memory operations are treated as an MDP. A tabular contextual bandit with UCB exploration learns from binary task-by-task success, with no extra LLM calls, when and how much to retrieve and when to inject a stored plan.
numbers: 6 benchmarks, 3 frameworks, 3 backbones. On GPT-4.1-mini the six-benchmark mean beats G-Memory by 2.6 to 4.2 points (42.6, 43.4, 43.7 vs 39.0, 40.8, 39.5) with 10.9 to 24.1% fewer input tokens. Best or tied best in 14 of 18 cells. Lobster-ALFWorld 59.7 to 67.9%. Trails the best baseline on ScienceWorld, TriviaQA and WebWalkerQA under LangGraph.
limits: Gains are modest and not uniform. Preprint, one author team. Arms are memory operations, not reasoning strategies. A search summary claimed up to 15.2 points; I did not find that figure in the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. A second case where learning from per-task success across items improves an agent. Both cases use code outside the model. Learning needs tens to hundreds of tasks to show a gain.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang and Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: In multi-armed bandits with the history in the prompt, models did not explore robustly. Only one configuration worked: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought and an externally summarised history given as sufficient statistics.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2; only one configuration out of all tried gave satisfactory exploration.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session. 2023-24 models and simple bandits. Newer reasoning models may do better; untested here.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. If an LLM is shown a raw log of past strategy outcomes it is likely to misuse it. Give it a pre-computed table (successes and tries per strategy and task type), not a transcript.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Select-then-Solve, self-routing result (same paper as d02)
finding: Letting the model choose its own paradigm zero-shot helps only the strongest model. Weaker models mostly pick tool paradigms whatever the task and fall below their Direct baseline.
numbers: Self-routing average 48.4% vs Direct 47.6%. GPT-5 67.1% (vs Direct 60.3% on the full set), Qwen3-Max 42.4%, Qwen3-30B 27.5%, both below their baselines. Self-routing picks: Qwen3-30B chose ReAct 48.0%, Qwen3-Max ReAct 42.4%; GPT-5 chose Direct 65.1%. The learned router chose Direct for 47 to 73% of tasks.
limits: A paradigm includes tool access, so a model that over-picks tools is partly misjudging the need for search. Single prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2. A prompted which-strategy-should-I-use step is not a reliable signal for weaker models. The switch decision should rest on a measured signal (disagreement, check result), not on the model's own choice.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Select-then-Solve, per-model paradigm effects (same paper as d02)
finding: For the strongest model, adding reasoning structure often buys nothing and can hurt, while weaker models gain more. Direct matches or nearly matches the best paradigm on knowledge and math tasks for GPT-5.
numbers: GPT-5: Direct 88% vs best 89% on MMLU; CoT 15 points below Direct on HumanEval (85 to 70); ReAct +44 over Direct on GAIA; Plan-Execute +32 on SEAL. Full-set Direct vs best fixed paradigm: GPT-5 60.3 vs 61.8, Gemini-Flash 48.0 vs 56.1, Qwen3-Max 41.3 vs 46.5, Qwen3-30B 21.9 vs 31.7.
limits: Tool access confounds the task-type effect. 2026 models, no per-paradigm prompt tuning.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. Supports the idea that strong models already do the standard strategies internally. Structure pays when it adds information (search, execution), not when it only restates reasoning.

source: Lin et al. (2026) disagreement routing, ablation and rewriting analysis (same paper as d03)
finding: The two arms of the router are complementary. Rewriting (reformulating the problem) helps hard items and hurts easy items; majority voting is the reverse. Combined they beat either arm alone.
numbers: Qwen3-8B ablation on Math500 / Olympiad / AIME24: baseline 84.4 / 46.4 / 36.7; only rewrite 90.4 / 59.0 / 56.7; only majority 87.6 / 48.6 / 40.0; full 92.8 / 61.9 / 66.7. Budget sweep on Math500: routed 91.6 (4 samplings), 92.8 (6), 91.8 (8) vs majority 87.4 / 87.6 / 87.8. GSM8K flat because only 1.5 to 2% of items stay in disagreement.
limits: AIME24 has 30 items. Rewrite is a paraphrase of the problem, a weak form of representation change.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2 and 6. Gives an operational easy/hard split by sample disagreement instead of an a priori structure test. A cheap stand-in for gap 6: if repeated attempts disagree, treat the item as ill-structured and change the representation.

source: Jonassen (1997) Instructional design models for well-structured and ill-structured problem-solving learning outcomes
finding: Search-result summary: well-structured problems have convergent solutions and apply a limited set of rules within well-defined parameters; ill-structured problems have several solutions and paths, fewer parameters that can be manipulated, and uncertainty about which rules apply. Jonassen (2000) later sorted eleven problem types along this continuum.
numbers: None extracted (no experiment).
limits: Not opened; read from a search summary only. The criteria are descriptive and give no scoring rule. The 2000 typology was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Gives checkable features for a classifier prompt (one correct answer? known rule set? parameters changeable? information missing?) but no validated test exists.

source: Funke (2010) Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
finding: Search-result summary: CPS developed in Europe over about 30 years as a branch of thinking and problem solving; Tailorshop and MicroDYN are the two assessment examples; the question whether CPS needs complex cognition is answered with a tentative yes. The Heidelberg repository copy did not download as a PDF here.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened; full text not retrieved. The Dorner criteria (complexity, connectivity, dynamics, intransparency, polytely) were read only as restated in the related-work section of d09.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Five features an item classifier could check (many variables, links between them, change over time, hidden state, conflicting goals). Only d09 uses them, and not as a classifier.

source: Unidentified 2025 LLM study on a Wisconsin Card Sorting style rule-switch task (search snippet)
finding: A search summary says that in a WCST-like task where the rule changes without notice, LLMs (except DeepSeek) beat people on total correct matches but made more perseverative than non-perseverative errors, the reverse of people, and held a found rule as well as people did.
numbers: Search snippet only; no figures. The URL is the nearest human WCST modelling paper returned, not the LLM paper; the LLM paper title and authors were not recovered.
limits: Not opened; study not identified. Lead only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Consistent with d05: holding a rule is fine, noticing it has changed is the weak point.
